We are halfway through, so let me throw you a curveball. What would you do if we said no?
Having thought about it a lot, I would apply again next year, with a stronger plan for the company.
Good, that was concise. Could you elaborate on the stronger plan?
Yes. Working with my head of planning this year, I would hand over more of the daily decisions.
And if your uncle disagreed with that? He sounds like a strong personality.
He is. Asked to choose between the plan and the relationship, I would protect both, and I would talk to him first.
You did not get sidetracked there. Can you recap your answer in one sentence?
Let me recap: I would apply again, delegate more, and bring my uncle into the plan before I start.

I never stop a mock interview in the middle, and candidates are often surprised by that. They want feedback after every answer. But practicing one question at a time does not show you what happens after twenty minutes, and the real interview is forty. Around minute twenty, most candidates change. Their answers get longer, the filler words come back, and they start to get sidetracked by stories that have nothing to do with the question. Nobody notices it in a short practice. So I run the whole thing as a dry run, from the first handshake to the last question, and I record it. At the end I ask for one thing: listen to the recording the next day and write down five changes. Not the same day. On the same day you hear what you meant to say. The next day you hear what you actually said.

I am an engineer, and before my interview I did three dry runs with a coach. The first recording was a shock. My answer about my career took four minutes, and I said the word basically nineteen times. So I made three changes. First, every first answer had to fit in ninety seconds. If they wanted more, they would ask me to elaborate. Second, every time I wanted to say basically or um, I made a short pause instead. It felt strange, but on the recording it sounded calm. Third, I ended every long answer with a one-sentence recap. Months later, a friend on the admissions committee told me what my interviewer had written: that I came across as calm and concise, and that I thought on my feet. I laughed, because three weeks before, none of that was true.
